Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verse 1:

﴿Wash-shamsi wa duhaha﴾ ... ﴿man dassaha﴾

Here Allah swears by certain cosmic creations and phenomena, and in the same way He swears by the creation of the human soul, by its being proportioned and perfectly balanced, and by the inspiration of good and evil into it. The purpose of this oath is that these creations of God should become significant, that people should attach importance to them, and that by reflecting on these things they should come to know their importance and worth, what signs they give, and what indications of divine power lie in them, so that they may understand for what reasons Allah has sworn by them.

It is a fact that there is a dialogue between the human heart and these scenes of nature. Between the two there is a particular hidden language, which exists in the depths of deep human consciousness and human nature. Between these scenes, whatever they may be, and human nature and consciousness there is also a profound harmony, and a dialogue continues between the two, without any sound being produced or any needle being placed upon a record. These scenes speak to the heart, and they have signs directed toward the human spirit, and within them there flows a life which is familiar with and converses with a living human being. Whenever a living person encounters these scenes, he will find in them feelings of love and intimacy toward himself, and these scenes will accompany him in perfect harmony and will convey their message to him in their own particular language.

This is why the Holy Qur'an, in many ways and through various styles, draws human attention to the observation of the cosmos, and it does not let any opportunity in this regard pass. Sometimes the Qur'an directly gives the guidance to reflect upon these scenes of nature, and sometimes through incidental indications, as here, by swearing by certain creations and certain scenes, it points out that these scenes too lie within the framework of the realities to come. In this final section we have repeatedly noted that such guidance and indications are very numerous. There is no surah in which there is not this guidance and this indication: look closely at the book of the universe, seek out the harmony and signs within this universe, converse with this universe in its particular language, and listen to its argument.

﴿Wash-shamsi wa duhaha﴾ (91:1): "By the sun and its brightness." Here the sun and its forenoon (duha), the time of chasht (mid-morning), and the emergence of sunlight are sworn by. When the sun rises and its light spreads fully, at that time it is extremely beautiful, extremely good, indeed pleasant and sweet, and in winter people gain warmth in the sunlight at that time, and this time is of extreme pleasantness. In summer too it is the time of ishraq (sunrise brightness), it is beautiful, and it is the time before the harsh heat of midday. In short, at chasht time the sun shines forth with its complete beauty. Some narrations state that the chasht time here means the whole day, but I think that why should we take the whole day, going beyond the time of duha and its literal meaning, since at the time of chasht there are greater indications of beauty and pleasantness, as we said earlier.

By the moon when it follows it (91:2). That is, it comes after the sun: when the sun sets, its subtle, transparent, beautiful and pure light appears. There is an ancient bond of love between the human heart and the moon, and this bond has gone deep into human nature; in human psychology and conscience, in the human heart and consciousness, it appears alive and luminous. Then the moon also holds a pleasant and affectionate dialogue with the human heart, gives loving signs, and in it there is also the praise of the Creator. It is close to the point that a listening person, hearing the praise of the bright moon, [finds it so]; sometimes, when a sensitive heart reflects on a moonlit night, it perceives in that deep light of the moon the being and bounties of Allah, and in those luminous waves it washes away the rust of consciousness, quenches its thirst, and pressing its breast to that light, it is immersed in the light of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verse 3:

﴿وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا جَلَّاهَا﴾ (91:3): "And by the day when it reveals it (the sun) in full display." In this verse there is an indication that (ḍaḥāhā) refers to a limited time, not the whole day, and the pronoun in (jallāhā) refers to the sun, which is mentioned in this context. However, the context here indicates that what is meant is "the earth." In the Qur'an this style has often been adopted, where a pronoun refers to something that, although not mentioned in the context, is known in the mind and is always present in human consciousness. Here the demands of the context are that the pronoun's referent be the earth. Thus the day illuminates this earth and people see it well. The role of the day in human life is known to all. The condition of man is that, having continually enjoyed the pleasures of day and night, he has forgotten their taste. Thus here, by showing a glimpse of the cycle of night and day, an attempt has been made to renew its beauties in the human heart, so that by reviving and sharpening human sensibilities he may be made to enjoy this scene.

By the night when it covers (over). Here the word yaghshaha, "covers," is used in contrast with jallaha, "reveals and brightens." The reason is that the night gathers all things to its bosom, covering and concealing them. This is a scene that deeply affects the human heart, and just as daylight has its effects on human life, so too does the night have its effects.

After this, an oath is sworn by the sky, its structure, and its construction.

By the sky and He who built it. [Here "ma" in Arabic grammar turns the verb that follows it into a verbal noun (masdar).] When we speak of the sky, we understand it to be a blue dome above our heads. When we look at this dome, we see stars and planets scattered within it, and planets moving through its spaces and orbits. What is its reality? We do not know the true reality. What we see above our heads is like a magnificent building, joined together and extremely strong. How this great hall is constructed, and how its parts are joined together so that they do not scatter, we do not know. They float in a space whose beginning and end we do not know. This is the thing whose reality we do not know. Whatever the people of knowledge have written about the sky until now are only theories, and they are subject to amendment and refutation. These theories have never stood firm on their own feet in any age, and they have always lacked stability and permanence. Our view and our faith, which is the strongest, is that the hand of divine power holds them.

Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him (Qur'an 35:41). It is Allah who holds the heavens and the earth from slipping away, and if they were to slip, none other than Allah could hold them in place. This is the knowledge that is most firmly established; there is no other certain matter beyond it.

After this comes the oath by the earth and by its being spread out.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verse 6:

﴿وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا طَحَاهَا﴾ (91:6) "And by the earth and He who spread it out." Ṭaḥā is derived from ṭaḥw, which means to spread out, just as ad-daḥw means to spread out and to make smooth for life. This is a great and manifest reality, on which the life of humans and of all animals depends. The harmony that Allah has created within the heavens and the earth is the blessing by which life has become possible here, and all of this has happened solely by the planning and measure of Allah. For us, this clear and apparent reality is sufficient: if any one of these properties and harmonies were to be disturbed, then neither would life exist on this earth, nor would it continue in this manner. The word ṭaḥw used here, or ad-daḥw used in Surah An-Nazi'at (79:30), ...

﴿وَالْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ دَحَاهَا * أَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَاهَا﴾ (79:30–31) "And the earth, after that, He spread it out, and brought forth from it its water and its pasture." Both meanings are spreading out, and this spreading out is among the greatest of these harmonies. It is a clear work of the hand of divine power. By mentioning this spreading out here, a pointer is made to the power of God, and the human heart is prompted to reflect upon it and take admonition.

After these oaths and the phenomena of the cosmos and the scenes of nature contained within them, the great realities of the human self are now presented, because among the wonders of this universe, this is the greatest wonder, which subsists by virtue of these harmonies of the heavens and the earth.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verses 7–8:

Surah Ash-Shams 91:7–10: "And the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness. He has certainly succeeded who purifies it, and he has certainly failed who instills it [with corruption]." In these four verses the Islamic view of the soul (nafs) is stated. It is also alluded to in the preceding surah, Surah Al-Balad.

﴿And We showed him the two paths﴾ (90:10). Also in Surah Al-Insan the same point is alluded to.

﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful﴾ (76:3). The summary of this view is that the human soul, by its nature, has two capacities, as is stated in Surah Sad.

﴿And mention when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] soul, then fall down to him in prostration"﴾ (38:71–72). What is said above about the human soul is also connected with the Islamic doctrine of individual responsibility, as is stated in Surah Al-Muddaththir.

﴿Every soul is pledged for what it has earned﴾ (74:38). This subject is also connected with the verse which says that Allah deals with every human being according to his deeds, as is stated explicitly in Surah Ar-Ra'd.

﴿Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ (13:11). In all these verses we learn what the view of Islam and the Qur'an regarding the human being is, and what the features of the human being are.

The summary is that this creature has two aspects within itself. Its capacities also have two directions; within its essence are two capacities. By this we mean that one aspect of its creation is material, namely the clay from which it was made, and the second aspect is that of the spirit which was breathed into it, and this spirit is the spirit of Allah. Thus the capacity of the clay leads toward evil, and the capacity of the spirit leads it toward good. By its creation it can move toward good and evil, guidance and misguidance, and it has also been given the faculty of distinguishing good from evil, and it has been given the choice to turn its soul toward good or toward evil. This power, choice and capacity exist within it by virtue of its creation. The Qur'an has pointed to this at one time by the word "inspiration" (ilham).

﴿And the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ (91:7–8). And at another time the Qur'an has pointed to it by the word "guidance" (hidayah).

﴿And We showed him the two highways﴾ (90:10). So this capacity has been placed within the essence of this creature by virtue of its creation. All the struggles of the messengers, the guidance of all good people, and all external influences and factors in truth awaken this capacity, give it a direction and a course, and sharpen or dull it. External factors do not create this capacity, because this capacity, a two-directional capacity, by the nature of creation, by the disposition, and by divine inspiration, exists within the human being.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verses 9–10:

﴿Certainly he succeeds who purifies it, and he fails who corrupts it.﴾ The meaning is that, apart from these natural powers and capacities, there is within man a faculty of perception (quwwat mudrikah), and by virtue of this faculty man has been created as a responsible being. The person who uses this faculty of perception to purify the self and to increase within it the capacity for goodness, and who lets the capacity for good prevail over the evil, is the one who succeeds. And the person who darkens his rational faculty, conceals it, suppresses it and weakens it, is the one who fails.

In short, man's responsibility arises from the fact that he possesses the rational faculty and the faculty of perception, and through this faculty he can give direction to the capacities for good and evil that exist within the self. By placing these capacities in the field of good he can nurture them, and by placing them in the field of evil he can nurture evil. As a consequence of this freedom and choice, responsibility has been laid upon man. Obligation has been imposed upon his power. This is a gift, in return for which obligations have been placed upon him.

But God is most merciful. Man has not been left merely to his natural aptitude, his rational faculty of perception, and his innate inspiration and guidance. Rather, from Adam (peace be upon him) to Muhammad (ﷺ), messengers were sent for this guidance, who continually laid down for them permanent values. They taught mankind the fundamental matters of faith and explained the proofs of faith and guidance. They explained, through the proofs within the human self and the signs on the horizons of this universe, the matters of faith. They continually lifted the veils of misguidance from human eyes so that the right path would appear correctly to them. And so that this path would be known to man as clear, plain and without any confusion, they set up milestones everywhere, so that the human being might reach the goal and walk the path he is to tread with insight. Whichever path he chooses, he walks upon it.

This, in brief, is God's plan and purpose for man. Whatever occurs, occurs within its sphere; it occurs in accordance with the will of God and within the complete system of divine decree.

This brief commentary on the status and dignity of man and on humanity contains extremely valuable points which are very beneficial for human refinement and training. First, through it, the human being is declared a highly honoured and dignified creature, in that he is regarded as independent and responsible for his own affairs. Although this authority and responsibility lie within the broader system of God's will and decree, since it was God's will that granted him this freedom and authority, nonetheless it definitely determines his station and rank, and he is established as a free and self-determining creature. Thus, in this universe, man occupies an exceedingly lofty and exalted position, because he is a creature which God fashioned with great care, then breathed into him of His spirit, and preferred him over many and most of the other creatures of this world.

The second important point is that these verses establish that man is himself responsible for his end. The entire matter has been placed in his hands (within the sphere of divine will, as we have explained). This responsibility gives rise in his consciousness to a colour of caution and taqwa. He knows that God's decree will operate in his person in the same way that he directs his own actions and activities.

﴿Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.﴾ In truth, this is an extremely great responsibility. No conscious person can remain heedless of it or careless about it.

The third point is that it creates in human thought the awareness that, in order to remain steadfast upon the right path, he should turn to God's permanent standards and eternal values, so that he is certain that his desires have not led him onto wrong paths or deceived him, lest his desires cast him onto the road of destruction. And lest, as a consequence of divine decree, he should have already made his desire into his god. For this reason, by being obedient to the Shariah in this way, he will never stray from the paths of God. He will be walking in accordance with God's guidance, and will receive light from that illumination which God has bestowed upon him to walk those dark paths of the world.

Accordingly, God has provided man with countless means for purifying the self and cleansing the essence, so that he may reach Him. Around him flow rivers of light; he can bathe in them at all times, and in the springs of knowledge of the Creator that flow throughout this universe he can purify his own essence.

After this, through a living historical example, the matter is clarified: how man buries his self under the pollutions of the world, and then deprives it of the path of guidance. This example is the people of Thamud, who became deserving of God's wrath, upon whom a severe punishment descended, and who were destroyed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 91, verses 11–15:

کذبت ثمود ................................ عقبھا

The story of the people of Thamud and their Prophet, Salih (peace be upon him), comes in the Qur'an at several places. We have discussed it at each place, and just now in Surah al-Fajr, in this same part (para), this story has passed. The details can be seen at those places.

Here it is only stated that the people of Thamud denied their Prophet solely because of their rebelliousness, and they had no other justification for it than this rebelliousness. The event happened thus: one of them, a most hard-hearted person, rose up and slew the she-camel of Allah. This man was among them the most cruel and rebellious, so that he became ready to commit such a great crime. Yet their Prophet had clearly warned them and had said that they should not cause any harm to this she-camel, nor interfere with the water which Allah has divided between you and the she-camel, so that one day is for you and one day is for the she-camel. This division had come about because they had demanded a miracle from the Prophet of Allah, and so Allah made this she-camel a miracle. Some miraculous quality of this she-camel there certainly was. Here we do not go into its details, because Allah Himself has not given the details of that miraculous quality. In any case, because of their rebelliousness they denied the warner sent by Allah, and they slew the she-camel. The one who actually carried out this deed took upon himself this act, and he was among them far more wretched and evil. But the responsibility was taken by all of them. All of them were held responsible because they did not restrain that man from this evil act, but rather encouraged him. It is a fundamental principle of Islam that in the collective life of the world, responsibility is also collective, and this law of collective responsibility is not contrary to the principle of individual responsibility in Islam. That is to say, on the Day of Judgment no person will bear the burden of another, and every person will receive only what he has earned; for in Islam it is also a major sin for someone to abandon advising others, to turn away from reforming others and supporting them, and not to encourage people to do good and to seize the hand of the oppressor.

When they committed this great crime, then the hand of divine power came into motion.

فدمدم علیھم ............................ فسوھا (14:91) "Finally, because of their sin, their Lord brought down upon them such a calamity that He levelled them all to the dust together." "Damdama" means wrath, and the vengeance and punishment that come as a result of wrath. The very pronunciation of the word "damdam" shows how severe that punishment would be. The pronunciation and the rhythm of this word itself point toward a frightening scene. Allah turned their land upside down and leveled it. This is a depiction which expresses an extremely all-encompassing destruction.

ولا یخاف عقبھا (15:91) "And He does not fear its consequence." He is free from every weakness; how could He fear anyone? Where could He be apprehensive, and when could He be fearful?

In fact, through this manner of expression, a necessary implication is pointed out: that Allah's grip is extremely severe, because whoever in the world does not fear any consequence will inflict the most severe oppression. Likewise, Allah's seizure will be severe, because there is no one to question Allah. This is why

ان بطش .................... لشدید "Surely the seizure of your Lord is very severe." By saying that He does not fear the evil consequence of any of His acts, the intention is to show that the seizure of Allah will be very severe.

In this way the human soul is connected with the great truths of this universe, and the human soul is linked with the sights and scenes of this universe. Then both the human soul and the sights of the universe are connected with that Sunnah of Allah which He has established for seizing the rebellious and those who deny. All these events happen within the bounds of Allah's decree, in whose system Allah has appointed a time for everything. Every calamity has a fixed time. Every event has a purpose, and in the system of this decree divine wisdom is operating at every single step. This is because Allah is the Lord of the soul, the Lord of this universe, and He is also the sole administrator of the system of qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination). Therefore, all of these are within the scope of His vast overall plan of will.
